newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Car sector, Asia dictate rubber's future-officials.
newsitem.headline: Car sector, Asia dictate rubber's future-officials.

text.p: The world supply of rubber will continue to outstrip demand in the near term, with the automobile industry and Asia's top three growers of the crop dictating market direction, a conference heard on Wednesday.
But prices were difficult to predict as current rates were already not reflective of fundamentals, said officials attending the Natural and Synthetic Rubber Markets '97 conference.

"As about two-thirds of the total world rubber consumption is in tyre manufacturing, the scenario of the elastomer market is exclusively determined by the transport and automobile industry," Abdul Aziz Kadir, director of the Rubber Research Institute of Malaysia, told the conference.
Abdul Aziz said it was also "immediately clear that Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia will remain the dominant growers of hevea (rubber) in the next two decades".
But he said rubber market prices had remained depressed despite shortfalls in supply. "There are no ready answers to explain away this imbalance in market behaviour."
World production of elastomers -- including synthetic rubber -- totalled 16,010,000 tonnes in 1996, against consumption of 15,920,000 tonnes.
"The level of consumption is expected to fall short of the peak level reached in the late 1980s," said Abdul Aziz.
The output ratio of natural rubber against synthetic rubber was currently at 40:60, though natural rubber has higher demand due to its durability in tyre-making, said officials.
Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia together produced about 85.2 percent of the world's natural rubber and Africa accounted for about 6.8 percent.
The bulk of the world's natural rubber was also consumed by rapidly-developing Asian countries.
Although prospects for rubber was already weak in Malaysia, investment opportunities were still attractive in Thailand and Indonesia, said officials.

"Thailand is expected to increase the rubber consumption in the country from 10 percent to 20 percent in 2000, due to the strong policy of the government," said Viyavoood Sincharoenkul and Wate Thainugal, president and manager, respectively, of the Thai Rubber Association, in a joint paper.

Ridwan Dereinda, senior researcher of Indonesia's Centre for Agrobusiness Development Research, said rubber growing was a major source of income for the country and domestic demand for the crop was enough to sustain good production.
